title: Go to each side (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 12)
hookLine: Aaron went to each side of a quarrel, telling each how sorry the other was
tomorrow: how small can a first step be and still count?

cards: Two friends at the same lunch table, eating with their shoulders turned half away from each other. Everybody feels it; nobody says it. You can almost hear the silence between them.
Then lunch ends, and they leave by different doors.
Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an old companion to the sayings of the sages, tells how Aaron, the brother of Moses, handled exactly this, and the answer to yesterday's question starts with where he sat down.

teach.b: When two people quarreled, Aaron went and sat down beside one of them. Sat: not a summons, not a lecture. And he said, my son, look at what your friend is going through.
He's tearing at his heart, ripping his clothes, saying: how can I lift my eyes and face my friend? I'm ashamed. I'm the one who wronged him.
Aaron stayed beside him until the anger left his heart.
Then he went and sat beside the other one, and said the same.
And when the two met, they embraced and kissed. The high priest of Israel, in this picture, spends his days on this: one quarrel at a time, one person at a time.
The midrash ties it to Aaron's death: the Torah says all the house of Israel wept for him. Now notice the senses in it. Sitting beside, not across.
Torn clothes. A hug at the end. Peace here is something a body does: Aaron walks to one side, then walks to the other.
The midrash doesn't say whether the friend had already said those words out loud; some readers hear yesterday's lesson in it, great is peace.
Here's the line to repeat tonight: in the Mishnah, Hillel says be among the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing it, rodef shalom.
Pursuing. You can't do that sitting still.

how: Jewish teaching holds up Aaron as the model peacemaker: Hillel's saying in Pirkei Avot, 'be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace', is often taught with this story, and making peace between people (shalom bayit, hava'at shalom) is counted as a mitzvah.

games.q: what does “go to each side” mean?
o: make peace by sitting with each person in turn
make peace by bringing both to a neutral judge
make peace by picking the side that is right

p: sat beside one, until the anger left
sat beside the other, said the same
all the house of Israel wept

s: Aaron's first move was to get both people into one room to talk
he went to each alone first; they met only after the anger had left.
the midrash connects Aaron's peacemaking to how all Israel mourned him
the Torah says all the house of Israel wept for him.
Hillel says to be among the students of Moses, loving peace
the students of Aaron: loving peace and pursuing peace.

games.q: two of your cousins stopped speaking after a family party. your aunt asks you to help. what's Aaron's move?
o: make a group chat with both and ask them to sort it out there.
post a quote about forgiveness and hope that both of them see it.
visit each one alone, listen, and tell each the regret you've seen.
games.why: Aaron sat beside each one separately, spoke to their shame and regret, and stayed until the anger left. only then did the two meet.

practice: Sit with an empty space beside you, and turn your shoulders a little toward it, the way Aaron sat next to each person rather than across from them.
Picture someone in a quarrel right now sitting there, and stay with them without fixing anything. Halfway through, turn the other way and sit beside the other side.

wordCard.voice: Go to each side: Aaron's way of making peace in Avot de-Rabbi Natan. Sit with one, then with the other, until the two can meet.

orig.note: Hebrew: one who pursues peace, as Hillel describes Aaron (Avot 1:12).

carryVoice: Keep this one: go to each side. Aaron didn't send a message across the room; he walked over and sat down.

sources.ref: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, chapter 12 (Aaron sits with each side of a quarrel until the anger leaves; they meet and embrace; Numbers 20:29)
Mishnah Avot 1:12 (Hillel: be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace)
Numbers 20:29 (all the house of Israel wept for Aaron)
